r2-p01-000: Low-Cost Bridge Vibration Anomaly Detection System Robust to Temperature and Humidity Changes
r2-p01-003: In April 2023, the walkway of the roughly 30-year-old Jeongja Bridge in Bundang collapsed during ordinary pedestrian use after corrosion and damage accumulated in its cantilever members, killing one person and injuring another. In January 2022, the Fern Hollow Bridge in Pittsburgh, USA, also collapsed during the morning commute after corrosion had been flagged in inspections but repairs were delayed. In both accidents, warning signs observed in inspections did not lead to repair or reinforcement, showing that periodic inspection alone cannot track changes in structural condition continuously enough to prevent accidents.
r2-p01-010: Independently of its size, a bridge's condition is rated by safety grade (A–E), and from December 2025 precision safety diagnosis was extended to aging and low-grade (C·D·E) facilities as well. Precision safety diagnosis, however, is costly and labor-intensive and is performed only on a fixed cycle — every 4 to 6 years depending on the safety grade — so a time gap remains between inspections, and changes in dynamic properties that accumulate during that gap are
r2-p02-000: hard to detect. As a result, aging small and medium bridges such as pedestrian overpasses and small footbridges lack a low-cost supplementary means of continuously detecting changes in condition between inspections.
r2-p02-003: Existing SHM (Structural Health Monitoring) systems install sensors on a structure permanently for continuous measurement, but they rely on precision equipment and dedicated infrastructure — ultra-precise piezoelectric accelerometers, high-performance data-acquisition hardware, distributed fiber-optic sensors (e.g., KRISS BOCDA) — and are therefore applied mainly to a few large, critical bridges such as Incheon Bridge; their cost and installation constraints make them impractical to deploy widely on small and medium aging bridges in service. Between periodic precision diagnosis and costly continuous measurement, low-cost continuous screening that precedes precision diagnosis is effectively missing. Bridge safety management therefore needs a multi-stage concept in which continuous screening (first stage) filters out anomaly candidates before precision safety inspection and diagnosis, so that limited inspection staff and budgets can be concentrated on suspect bridges.
r2-p02-005: This work addresses the three problems summarized above: ① capturing changes in dynamic properties continuously between inspections while separating environmental effects, ② the time gap between precision-diagnosis cycles, and ③ the difficulty of applying precision measurement systems to small and medium aging bridges. It is not a system that predicts collapse or replaces precision safety diagnosis; it is a low-cost first-stage (supplementary) screening system that fills the time gap between inspections and diagnoses by indicating which bridges should be inspected first.
r2-p02-006: The purpose of this work is to develop a low-cost, machine-learning-based bridge vibration screening system that addresses this blind spot and this missing technology at the same time, with three goals. First, vibration data are collected with an ADXL355Z MEMS accelerometer and a Raspberry Pi (3 Model A+ in stage 1, 5 in stage 2); because damage data cannot be created deliberately on a bridge in service, unsupervised learning trained only on normal data is used. Second, since a bridge's natural frequency rises and falls with air temperature and humidity even without damage [2], a DHT22 records temperature and relative humidity, and the normal temperature/humidity–natural-frequency relationship is learned so that variation explained by the environment is removed and false alarms are reduced. Third, because an anomaly signal alone does not tell an inspector where to look, the system implements explainable alarms that also show which frequency bands deviated from the normal baseline, guiding the direction of the follow-up precision inspection.
r2-p03-002: An SHM study combined a Raspberry Pi with a low-cost MEMS accelerometer (ADXL355) and showed that a structure's natural frequencies, mode shapes and damping can be identified without ultra-precise piezoelectric sensors costing tens of millions of won [1]. That study, however, focuses on identifying dynamic characteristics and does not address how environmental variables such as temperature and humidity, or changes in operational loading, affect anomaly detection.
r2-p03-009: The distinctiveness of this work therefore rests on three axes: direct low-cost hardware implementation, temperature/humidity compensation, and band-wise explainability. Unlike low-cost MEMS studies, it reduces false alarms through temperature/humidity compensation; unlike fiber-optic measurement, it performs continuous screening with inexpensive general-purpose parts; and unlike unsupervised studies that output only an anomaly score, it also reports the contribution of each band to the reconstruction error.
r2-p03-011: This system is a supplementary vibration-screening system for early detection of vibration-anomaly candidates in aging small and medium bridges, based on low-cost, low-power hardware and unsupervised learning. It collects vibration, temperature and relative humidity with an ADXL355Z-based MEMS accelerometer and a DHT22 temperature/humidity sensor, and aims to reduce environment-driven false alarms using the temperature/humidity–frequency relationship learned in the normal state. It then detects anomaly candidates that depart from the normal vibration pattern with Autoencoder-based unsupervised learning and, when an anomaly occurs, shows which frequency bands (or bands around modes) have large reconstruction errors, helping to prioritize precision inspection.
r2-p03-012: Our own experimental validation has two stages. Stage 1 confirms that the whole collection–compensation–detection–explanation pipeline works, using a foam-board model and manual excitation; stage 2 overcomes stage 1's two limitations (indistinct resonance peaks and variation in manual excitation) with an aluminum multi-span model and
r2-p04-000: a solenoid auto-tapper, validates discrimination performance on a matrix of temperature, humidity, mass and bolt-loosening conditions, and builds a real-time measurement and analysis setup based on a Raspberry Pi 5 (details in 2.2 and 3.1).
r2-p04-020: The core measurement and processing hardware — ADXL355Z evaluation board ₩84,589, DHT22 sensor ₩5,680 and Raspberry Pi 5 (about ₩100,000 for the 2–4 GB RAM model) — costs about ₩190,000 in total. This is far below existing SHM measurement that presupposes ultra-precise piezoelectric accelerometers and dedicated acquisition equipment (based on piezoelectric sensors costing tens of millions of won; see 1.3 and [1]), supporting this work's goal of a low-cost configuration that can be deployed on many small and medium bridges.
r2-p04-022: The software analysis unit consists of two programs, one for acquisition and one for analysis. The acquisition program runs in Python on the Raspberry Pi and writes the ADXL355Z 3-axis acceleration at 200 Hz (500 Hz in stage 2) and the DHT22 temperature and relative humidity at about 2-second intervals to a single CSV file. The analysis program splits this file into time windows and performs, in order, FFT and feature extraction, residual calculation by multivariate regression on temperature T and relative humidity RH, standardization, reconstruction-error-based anomaly scoring, a 99th-percentile threshold decision, and band-contribution output.
r2-p05-000: On the stage-2 aluminum model, every position is defined along the length of the deck (overall length 600 mm) with x = 0 at the left end. The solenoid tapper strikes the centerline of the top surface at mid-span, x = 300 mm, so that every tap consistently excites the first mode, and the gap between tip and deck is held at 2–5 mm with a card gauge in all conditions so that they touch only at the moment of impact. The ADXL355Z is attached to the underside of the deck at x = 240 mm, away from directly below the impact point, to measure the large bending response near mid-span while avoiding the local impact component right after the tap and interference from the weights and the impact point on top. Weights are placed at x = 150 mm (L/4) and x = 450 mm (3L/4), the same proportions as in stage 1.

r2-p05-004: 1. Vibration and temperature/humidity acquisition: 3-axis acceleration is collected from the ADXL355Z, and temperature T and relative humidity RH from the DHT22. The actual natural-frequency range was checked in a preliminary test so that the analysis band stays within the Nyquist limit, and the plan was to raise the sampling rate to 500 Hz if the measured first natural frequency approached or exceeded the 100 Hz Nyquist limit of 200 Hz sampling. On the stage-2 aluminum model, preliminary measurement after assembly showed the first natural frequency above that limit, so the sampling rate was fixed at 500 Hz and the measurement range at ±8 g (measured natural frequencies are given in 3.4). Excitation is by manual tapping in stage 1 and by automatic taps from the solenoid auto-tapper in stage 2 (at a fixed period after warm-up); tap times are logged on the same clock, and only the free-vibration segment right after each tap is used as the unit of analysis.
r2-p05-005: 2. Signal preprocessing and frequency-band feature extraction: the DC offset is removed from the acceleration signal and the spectrum is estimated (FFT/STFT in stage 1; in stage 2 the Welch method, which reduces noise by averaging spectra over short segments). RMS, standard deviation, peak-to-peak, peak frequency and power, band energies and so on are computed per segment and axis, and the analysis bands are reset to match the measured first natural frequency (stage 1: 0–12, 12–25, 25–50 Hz based on the preliminary 22.6 Hz peak; stage 2: 0–40, 40–80, 80–125 Hz based on the measured 101 Hz — see 3.4).
